# Mastoiditis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Head and neck surgery > Mastoiditis*

[Original Article Link](/library/kD0meR)

---

## Summary

Mastoiditis is an infection of the <u>mastoid air cells</u> that typically develops as a complication of <u>acute otitis media</u> (<u>AOM</u>) and most commonly occurs in children < 2 years of age. <u>Clinical features of mastoiditis</u> include <u>otalgia</u> and tender, <u>erythematous</u> postauricular swelling with <u>lateral</u> and forward displacement of <u>the ear</u>. <u>Fever</u> and <u>otorrhea</u> may be present. Diagnosis is clinical, but imaging is indicated in the case of diagnostic uncertainty, suspected intracranial complications, and/or failure to respond to initial treatment. Management involves intravenous <u>antibiotics</u> and symptomatic management; surgical options are based on the extent of infection. Complications include spread of the infection to nearby structures (e.g., the <u>brain</u>). <u>Chronic mastoiditis</u>, a subtype of mastoiditis with a more indolent course, can occur as a complication of <u>chronic otitis media</u>. Management includes <u>antibiotics</u> and sometimes <u>surgery</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

Most commonly occurs in children < 2 years [[1]](/library/awdQhH0)



Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Pathophysiology

Infection spreads from the <u>middle ear</u> cavity into the mastoid, which is a closed bony compartment → collection of <u>pus</u> under tension and <u>hyperemic</u> resorption of the bony walls → destruction of the air cells (coalescent mastoiditis) → mastoid becomes a <u>pus</u>-filled cavity (<u>empyema</u> mastoid)

---

## Clinical features

### Signs and symptoms [[1]](/library/awdQhH0)[[3]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* <u>Otalgia</u>

* Tender, <u>erythematous</u>, and <u>edematous</u> mastoid

* <u>Ear</u> displaced laterally and forward

* <u>Otorrhea</u>

* <u>Hearing loss</u>

* Systemic symptoms (e.g., <u>fever</u>, fatigue, irritability)

* Features of <u>complications of mastoiditis</u> (e.g., <u>facial nerve palsy</u>) [[3]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Symptoms of AOM</u> for > 2 weeks

* Obliteration of the retroauricular sulcus in advanced stages





### <u>Otoscopy</u>




* Bulging and <u>erythematous</u> <u>tympanic membrane</u>

* Normal in 10% of affected individuals [[3]](/library/AN1Rdh0)





> [!TIP]
> Suspect mastoiditis in patients with recent or persistent <u>otitis media</u> and <u>erythema</u>, swelling, <u>pain</u> behind <u>the ear</u>, and/or protrusion of the <u>pinna</u>. [[4]](/library/n8c7MV0)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Chronic mastoiditis</u> typically has mild symptoms and develops slowly; patients may be afebrile and clinically well. [[5]](/library/KBdUbs0)

## Diagnosis

### Approach




* Diagnosis is primarily clinical. [[1]](/library/awdQhH0)

* <u>Signs of sepsis</u>: Obtain <u>blood cultures</u>. [[1]](/library/awdQhH0)

* Effusion or <u>otorrhea</u>: Consult otolaryngology for consideration of culture from the <u>middle ear</u>. [[5]](/library/KBdUbs0)

* Order imaging if: [[6]](/library/NBd-as0)

* No symptom improvement after 48 hours of treatment

* Diagnostic uncertainty

* Suspected intracranial complication

* Planned surgical intervention





> [!TIP]
> Laboratory findings (e.g., <u>CBC</u>, <u>inflammatory markers</u>) are nonspecific. Normal <u>WBC</u> and <u>inflammatory markers</u> do not rule out mastoiditis. [[1]](/library/awdQhH0)




### Imaging




* <u>CT scan</u> of the <u>temporal bone</u> with contrast: initial imaging study  [[1]](/library/awdQhH0)

* Opacification of the <u>mastoid air cells</u>  [[1]](/library/awdQhH0)

* <u>Erosion</u> of the air <u>cell walls</u>

* <u>Pus</u> in the mastoid cavity (areas of <u>enhancement</u> on CT)

* <u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u> and <u>temporal bone</u> with contrast: Consider as initial modality in children due to lack of <u>ionizing radiation</u>.  [[1]](/library/awdQhH0)[[7]](/library/SucyqV0)

* More sensitive for intracranial infectious complications

* Characteristic findings include increased fluid signal intensity in <u>mastoid air cells</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> Interpret imaging in conjunction with clinical symptoms; some findings such (e.g., opacification of the <u>mastoid air cells</u>) are also visible in acute and <u>chronic otitis media</u>. [[1]](/library/awdQhH0)

## Management

This section covers the management of acute mastoiditis. For management of chronic infections, see “<u>Chronic mastoiditis</u>.”




### Approach [[1]](/library/awdQhH0)




* Unstable patients: Initiate <u>immediate hemodynamic support</u>.

* Start empiric IV <u>antibiotic therapy</u>.

* Provide symptomatic management (e.g., <u>antipyretics</u>, <u>oral analgesia</u>).

* Assess for signs of complications (e.g., <u>meningitis</u>, <u>cranial nerve</u> involvement)

* Consult otolaryngology for consideration of <u>surgery</u>.

* Adjust <u>antibiotics</u> based on clinical response and culture results.





### <u>Empiric antibiotic therapy</u> for acute mastoiditis [[1]](/library/awdQhH0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)




* Patients without either <u>chronic otitis media</u> or recent <u>antibiotic</u> use

* <u>Ampicillin/sulbactam</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[1]](/library/awdQhH0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* OR <u>ceftriaxone</u> DOSAGE [[1]](/library/awdQhH0)[[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* Patients with <u>chronic otitis media</u> or recent <u>antibiotic</u> use

* <u>Cefepime</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE

* OR <u>levofloxacin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE

* OR <u>piperacillin/tazobactam</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[1]](/library/awdQhH0)

* <u>Severe penicillin reaction</u>: <u>clindamycin</u> DOSAGE

* Suspected <u>MRSA</u>: Add <u>vancomycin</u> DOSAGE.

* Treatment duration is usually 2–4 weeks based on extent of disease. [[2]](/library/Bedza60)

* Transition to oral <u>antibiotics</u> when patients clinically improve. [[2]](/library/Bedza60)





### <u>Surgery</u> [[1]](/library/awdQhH0)




Options include:




* <u>Myringotomy</u> with or without <u>tympanostomy</u> tube insertion

* <u>Mastoidectomy</u>: in severe or refractory mastoiditis (e.g., bone destruction)

* <u>Incision and drainage</u>

* <u>Debridement</u>

---

## Complications

Untreated, the infection may spread through the bony walls and cause the following complications:




* Postauricular abscess

* Most common type

* <u>Pus</u> collects under the <u>skin</u> behind <u>the ear</u>.

* Pushes the <u>auricle</u> forward and downward

* Bezold abscess

* <u>Pus</u> breaks the tip of the mastoid and dissects into the neck, often collecting behind the <u>sternocleidomastoid</u>.

* Causes <u>neck pain</u>, <u>torticollis</u>, and <u>fever</u>

* Treatment: IV <u>antibiotics</u>, <u>mastoidectomy</u>, and drainage of neck <u>abscess</u>

* Zygomatic abscess

* Infection spreads to the zygomatic air cells (located at the zygomatic root)

* Causes swelling in front of and above the <u>auricle</u>

* <u>Brain abscess</u>: manifests as <u>fever</u>, <u>focal neurological deficits</u>, and signs of <u>raised intracranial pressure</u>

* <u>Cranial nerve palsies</u>: <u>abducens nerve</u>, <u>facial nerve</u>, and the <u>ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve</u>





We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
